utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. This morning, there are two matters I would like to bring to the attention of the parties. The first one is Judge Argibay won't be able to join us. In accordance with the Rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the remaining Judges decided to continue the proceedings. The second matter is the scheduling arrangement. According to our plan, we are going to have a break from 13th to 17th of October, and on the 20th, we will have another group of witnesses from the Prosecution. So we have to finish the testimony of these two witnesses before the 10th of October. Yesterday, Mr. McCloskey has promised me that he will do his best to finish his direct examination this morning. Could I ask Mr. Karnavas, how long are you going to take for your cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My estimation is five to six days. It could be a little bit longer, it could be shorter. It all depends on how disputive the witness is. If he is willing to give the answers forthrightly, it could even be shorter. But less than four days I would say would be very difficult because we have a lot of information to go through, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could you tell me exactly how many hours do you need because, you know, the Prosecution used about ten hours 30 minutes if they finished the direct this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, I can't tell you the exact amount of hours, but I could answer the question. Mr. Nikolic has given several different statements. There are also some additional information that was provided. There are also things that he has mentioned that now that would require me to go into depth into the rules and the regulations. Because of that, and there are a lot of inconsistencies, at least throughout the various versions that he has given, there are also some information that we have regarding his character which we believe directly relate to his propensity for dishonesty which we believe would be relevant to this Court. So in light of that, I would say I would need probably twice the amount of time that the Prosecution has put on. I intend to be as efficient as I possibly can be, you know, and I certainly do not intend to prolong it any longer than I have to but there is some information that we must go through. For example, when he indicates that he has a particular function, I need to go into the rules to demonstrate what his exact functions are. Also, the Prosecution opened some doors which require me to delve into in order for the Court to have a complete context of the situation. So in light of that, Your Honour, I don't think you can say that the Prosecution took ten hours then I should have ten hours because if they choose not to put in information that would tend to show his dishonesty, then it prevents me from showing that. So -- But you will see, Your Honour, we are eminently prepared, I will be as streamlined as I possibly can be and as laconic as I can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as you said, as a rule of this Tribunal, we'll give more or less the equal amount of time in the cross as to the direct. I believe that this witness is very important, very material to your case, and you need some time to cross-examine this witness. But you have to remember that the Bench has the power to shorten the time used by the parties for the direct or cross-examination. Since this witness is very material to your case, maybe we'll not sit tomorrow, and you'll have the whole day to prepare or reorganise your cross-examination. I hope you could finish your cross in 12 to 15 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that with or without the breaks, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course, without break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So in this case, on Thursday, 25th, we will sit in the morning from 9.00 to 1.45, and 3.00 to 4.30. And as well as on Friday, we also go from 9.00 to 1.45, and in the afternoon, 3.00 to 4.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, how long do you think you are going to use for the cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, judging by the relationship between the testimony of Mr. Nikolic and the Defence of Dragan Jokic, we have focussed on three groups of issues that we wish to clarify on the cross-examination of the witness. And we judge that that will take about 1 hour, 45 minutes. In other words, one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Anyway, we'll have the next witness on next Wednesday. That is Mr. Obrenovic. And how long do you think, Mr. McCloskey, your direct examination will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I may be able to finish in one day, but certainly no longer than two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, could I ask just a clarification. I know in the past you have mentioned you did not want witnesses to be surprised by new documents or new materials. Mr. Karnavas's comment regarding some sort of character evidence sounds like he has something new in mind outside the documents that we've all been living with for months, if not years now. So I was wondering if you could clarify for us what kind of discovery in the context of this witness you would expect the Defence to be able to provide, either the witness or the Prosecution, on new areas that he may be planning to go into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, you have to know that in the discovery of the evidence are different between the direct examination and cross-examination. During the cross-examination, the Defence could use whatever documents possible at their hands which does not constitute the surprising attack at all. But in order to facilitate the proceedings and to -- especially for the Trial Chamber to know which documents the Defence is going to use, we hope, we hope, that the Defence could provide us with those documents which they are going to use during the cross-examination to the Bench and to the other party before the cross-examination or before using those documents. Otherwise, we will spend a lot of time finding those documents which somehow is a surprising attack. Am I right? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I could not agree with you more, Your Honour. I just didn't want a pre-emptive strike coming from the Prosecution and that's why I want to let them complete their direct examination. We will present the documents, they will have it, and of course if they have any objections, they can raise it on the order and we can deal with it. It might sound like a surprise, but in essence, I don't believe it's my obligation to provide them with my cross-examination, telegraph what I'm going to do so they begin to do their rebuttal before I do my cross. So that's the whole purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So it seems that the direct examination of Mr. Obrenovic will take one day or at the most two days. I think the Defence of Mr. Jokic is allowed to have an equal period of time for the cross-examination. So we decided on the 3rd of October, Friday, we are not going to sit. Having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one minor matter to bring up and it deals with yesterday's translation. It became aware to us that when a question was posed and an answer given, that perhaps there might have been an error, and I underscore might have been an error in the translation of the answer provided by Mr. Nikolic. If you wish for me to deal with it through the legal officer, I could do that, or should I go on the record? I don't know the exact procedure you wish for me to proceed on this matter to make the correction, or at least to have them look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think everything should go publicly. And you may raise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may be right or you may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I'm not saying that they're wrong. I'm just saying that it was our impression that perhaps there was one minor error. It's on page 40 of the transcript. The question begins with line 21, and the time period is 12.44.37. The question was: "Did he do anything to encourage your continued involvement in these events that evening? Did he say or do anything that evening to encourage your continued involvement in this operation to move out the women and children and detain and kill the men?" That was the question posed by Mr. McCloskey. The answer was, and this is on line 25, it begins on line 25, and the time period is 12.45, 05: "No he didn't say anything along these lings that would give me the impression that he was encouraging me to do anything other than that." It is our belief that what he actually -- what the gentleman actually said was "anything like this" or "anything like that." In other words, they have interpreted to say that he encouraged me to do anything other than that, other than that. And we believe that the gentleman indicated that it was "anything like this," that he would encourage him to do anything like this. So that's on line 1, page 41, 12.45.09 is the time period. If they could look into, we would most appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas, to bring this matter to our attention. It is an important issue, but it's a matter of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will ask the interpreters to check the transcript and the tape recorder about the translation of this phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We appreciate that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, good morning. Just two little issue that is I need to address, one is if we are continuing with new witnesses on October 20th, can the Court please, would the Court please set a deadline for the Prosecution to provide us with some kind of witness list. We have no clue who the next witness is after Mr. Obrenovic, and we really can't be prepared by October 20th unless we have a witness list in the next couple of days. Second of all, I have notified the Prosecution that during the cross-examination of Mr. Obrenovic, we will be using an exhibit which is a model that's being built to the specifications of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. To eliminate any conflict or problems or objections when Mr. Obrenovic takes the stand, we would like to offer the Prosecution an opportunity to inspect the model, look at it, discuss it. We'll negotiate any problems they have with it. It will be available on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As for your first request, I think it's very legitimate. I think the responsibility lies on the shoulder of the Prosecution to inform the other parties the name and order of the next group of witnesses. I hope the Prosecution could do it as soon as possible. As for the second matter, I believe it's a good idea. Maybe the parties could discuss it after the sitting on this matter, and to see if there is any way out for this. If not, you are free to come back to the Bench. Thank you very much, Ms. Sinatra. We have lost about 20 minutes, but we'll try to make it up. But I hope we could finish the sittings this morning before 2.00. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Are you ready --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If possible, could we lower the ELMO a little bit. It's right between the witness and myself. Examined by Mr. McCloskey: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday when you had arrived back at the Bratunac Brigade in the early evening hours. You said it was still light on the 13th of July. At some point after that time, did you hear about an incident that occurred at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did hear that an incident had occurred at Kravica. But that wasn't that evening, but the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what time did you hear about the incident at Kravica warehouse the following day, on 14 July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it the following day in the morning. After having slept a part of the night, I was in town, and then I also heard about it when I came to the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you hear about it from first in town?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that already on the 14th, this was common knowledge. That is, almost the entire town, all the soldiers, had heard about it. People I saw and came across that day had heard that this incident had occurred in town. One of the people I heard about it from was the chief of the public security station, Miodrag Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the 14th, do you recall who you heard about it there from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the command of the Bratunac Brigade, in the operations room, the officers who were there, mostly members of the brigade command, were talking about it. Or rather, I discussed the incident with them, the incident I had heard about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your commander Mr. Blagojevic among those officers you discussed this with at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not able to confirm that now because this wasn't any meeting or debate or reporting. But since everyone knew about it, the whole town, I knew about it. Members of the brigade command knew about it. So all I can say is that Colonel Blagojevic must have known about it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question was if Mr. Blagojevic was among those officers. The gentleman then went on to speculate, to give what he believes Mr. Blagojevic would have known because he heard it, the intelligence officer heard it from others in the community. So I would appreciate if the gentleman would just answer the question. If Mr. McCloskey wishes to then pose another question, that's fine. But I think he's deliberately trying to bring out -- to make insinuations and speculations at this stage of the game, and he should know because he's here three days, and he should know that he's required to answer the question and only the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that from the answer of this witness, everything is quite clear because he said that he's really not able to confirm that because this wasn't any meeting or debate or reporting. But he thinks everybody knew about it. The whole town, I knew about it. Members of the brigade command knew about it. So all I can say is that Colonel Blagojevic must have known about it, too. It's quite clear. It's not speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, had he been asked the question do you know if Mr. Blagojevic was aware of it, I would not object to that. I do object to him going beyond the question and it forces me to make an objection. The question was very clear, was Blagojevic at that meeting? Answer is no. Mr. McCloskey can then ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there's a big problem in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What on the 14th of July had you learned occurred at the warehouse in Kravica, just if you can briefly tell us?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that on the previous day, that is, the 13th of July, 1995, an incident had occurred in a building known as OK Kravica in which among the Muslim prisoners, an automatic rifle was seized from a member of the police who was guarding them and who had captured them and was holding them there. And then the person who had grabbed the rifle shot at the policeman, and a police officer was killed. One or two others were wounded. And that after that, a group of policemen who were there used automatic weapons and other weapons they had on them to execute the prisoners in that facility. I also learned that in addition to the sidearms used to shoot at the captured Muslims in that facility, they brought boxes of hand grenades. They shut the doors. And then they killed the people inside using those grenades. I can also say that I heard that a witness of all those events and killings was Jovan Nikolic, who was the director of that cooperative, and that he, too, personally, when he objected to what they were doing, then he, too, was attacked and his life was imperiled. So that is what I heard briefly as to what had happened the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn what unit, from what police forces was involved in this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, I learned that elements of the special brigade of the MUP took part. Further, I learned that most of those who had taken part in the killings were members of the 2nd detachment from Sekovici. However, most of those were members of the MUP special police forces who were active in the area, in the Sandici village area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn approximately how many Muslims were murdered in this way at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The earliest information I had was several hundreds of Muslims. I don't know precisely, and I never really learned, the exact number of people who were killed. But the assessment was several hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A day or two later, I also heard that bodies from that killing site were buried by members of the MUP and that those bodies were buried in the Glogovi village area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the murders at the Kravica warehouse with your commander, Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that particular incident and the overall situation in the area, more specifically, the killing -- the killings at Kravica and those occurring along the road, we didn't speak officially at a meeting or anything. But we did discuss countless times the situation, and we discussed what was happening along the road as well as what had happened at Kravica. This was the subject of conversations both back in town and at the headquarters that I belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when you first spoke to your commander, Blagojevic, about the murders at Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the earliest, a day or two or three days after the killings at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive any instructions or information from him regarding the information you gave him about the killings at Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received no instructions, no assignments, not then, not at any time later for as long as I was a member of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever determine whether any Bratunac Brigade members were involved in the murders at Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After everything had happened, I looked into the problem of overall operations and everything that had happened in the Bratunac area. Throughout the period following these events, I obtained information that four persons, four individuals from Kravica, two of them members of the Bratunac Brigade, one of them a member of the MUP, I wasn't sure about the fourth -- the status of the fourth person there. I had information that those people had taken part in the killings at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information that they were part of an organised assignment at Kravica, or just they happened to go there as individuals?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information was that they had not been there as an organised group forming part of any unit. They were citizens of the Kravica local commune. And as such, they happened to be in the area and take part in the killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your review of the Kravica murders, did you identify any information that any member or members of the Bratunac Brigade Red Berets were part of the Kravica murders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe that the gentleman indicated he made a review. So if there's a foundation that needs to be made, I think Mr. McCloskey should lay it. Because he's learning -- he's talking about information that he learned. Now the question was, During your review - indicating there was a particular review as opposed to information coming in to an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think Mr. McCloskey, you need to go step by step so we could fully understand the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness did say that after these events, he looked into various events, including the Kravica warehouse. And that's all I meant by my word "review." And so I can try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we know the source of that information he obtained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the source of the information relating to specific members of the Bratunac Brigade being there at the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Your Honours, as an intelligence officer, it was my duty and within my purview to gather intelligence from such sources as I had previously defined as my colleagues, or rather collaborators. At Kravica, and throughout the Bratunac Brigade, I had people I worked with and they would cooperate with the security organ. I really can't bring into the public eye the names of the people I had then worked with. This was a duty. And we did have information on those events, and in general, the brigade was obtaining information on any events through the people providing information for us who were in direct contact with us throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As you've described when you looked into these -- the events at Kravica, at that time, did you receive any information that members or a member of the Bratunac Brigade Red Beret unit was present or involved at the Kravica massacre?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time. I had no information at that time concerning members of the Red Beret unit. I was able to obtain information. Later, I read a number of documents. But I can't say that at that time I had information that the Red Berets had taken part in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to documents that were provided you by the Prosecution in the discovery of this case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those are the documents I have in mind. And those documents indicated that there was a perpetrator at Kravica that was from the Red Beret unit of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you indicate what document or documents you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in mind a specific document talking about a member of the Red Berets having been wounded at Kravica during the killings, and that he was later transferred to the health centre in Bratunac or in Zvornik. I can't be sure right now. I no longer remember the document that clearly, but I think that's the document we both have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a document mentioned by Mr. Butler in his report. And since it was not something known to the witness at the time, I would just go on in my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- that that entire line of answers be disregarded at this point unless -- because he's just referring to a document that he read. He has no independent knowledge. So I'd ask that there be a finding of fact at this point in time that unless they can produce some verifiable information that would justify this line of questioning that the entire answer be disregarded and not be part of the finding of fact by this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the transcript is quite clear. And when we deliberate on the evidence at a later stage, we'll take your objections into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your discussions with Mr. Blagojevic about the Kravica warehouse massacres, did you ever mention that you had learned that Bratunac Brigade soldiers were involved?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did refer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when in this time frame that you informed your commander that you believed Bratunac Brigade soldiers were involved?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you the date specifically. But it was just after the killings had occurred. And the earliest date at which this would have been possible upon Mr. Blagojevic's return from Zepa, because at that time I had already obtained information as to what had happened concerning the killings at Kravica, the burials and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Kravica warehouse within the Bratunac Brigade zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, I'm not sure. It certainly was Bratunac Municipality. But in view of the battalion's position, I think it was behind the zone of responsibility of the 4th. I'm not really sure about the zones. I know what the battalions were covering, but whether that area was within the zone of responsibility, yes, it was just next to the zone of responsibility of the 1st and 4th Battalions. I'm simply not sure what is included in the zone of responsibility of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the evening of 13 July where you have told us that you went back to the brigade headquarters. What did you do that evening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I stayed for a while back at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. I went to my office. After that, I went to the mess to have dinner. Soon after that, I was contacted from the communications centre to go and speak to Colonel Beara at the -- in the centre of Bratunac town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime between 8.00 and half past 8.00 in the evening, I got in touch with Colonel Beara in the centre of town where the communications officers told me to report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you had any contact with Colonel Beara before meeting him that night in the centre of town, on this day or the day before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'd never had any contacts with him previously. But I did see him once, I believe, on the 13th in Bratunac. But up to that point, I had not been in personal contact with Colonel Beara, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before going to meet with Colonel Beara, did you have any idea what -- why he wanted to see you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no idea why he wanted to see me before I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you communicate with anyone in your command that you were going to go see Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't communicate with anyone. I had no idea why he wanted to see me, so there was no reason for me to inform anyone about that. I didn't tell anyone anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where in the centre of town did you meet with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bratunac, well, the main street, it's a small town and there's only one centre of town. There's a roundabout. Across the way from the roundabout, the offices occupied by political parties in town, the SDS and the other political parties. So that's the only centre of town there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him on the street, in an office, where?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the street quite literally in the centre, in the street, the town, the spot I just described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take anybody with you or were you by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we met, no, there was no one else with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it light out still or had it turned dark?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not dark yet. To the best of my recollection, it was between 8.00 and half past 8.00 in the evening. So it wasn't dark yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Colonel Beara say to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara ordered me to go to the command of the Zvornik Brigade and see Drago Nikolic personally that same evening. He also ordered me to convey his orders to Drago Nikolic that the Muslim prisoners in Bratunac would be transferred to Zvornik the same evening and that he should secure accommodation for those prisoners. Further, he told me to tell him to get his people ready because a lot of Muslim prisoners would be coming along. He also told me to convey these orders to Dragan Nikolic; namely, that the people who were to be transferred would be temporarily detained in buildings assigned by Dragan and that those people would be killed in the territory of Zvornik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is -- who was your understanding at that time was Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew who Drago Nikolic was even from before, before Colonel Beara told me to go and find him. Drago Nikolic was the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Colonel Beara tell you the approximate numbers of Muslims that would be shipped up to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't talk about specific numbers then, but he told me that all the Muslims who were in Bratunac would be transferred to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to hearing this from Colonel Beara, had you heard about the movement of the Muslims from Bratunac to Zvornik from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that evening. I didn't hear anything from anyone else. That was the first I heard about them being transferred to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do when he gave you this order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I switched on the engine of my car and drove town the Bratunac/Konjevic Polje/Drinjaca/Zvornik Road. I arrived at the Zvornik headquarters, that's at the reception. At the reception, I asked to speak to Drago Nikolic. I said that I was the chief of intelligence and security of the Bratunac Brigade. The janitor or guard who was there brought me to an office inside the headquarters. It was on one of the upper floors. I arrived there. I introduced myself, and I said that I needed to speak to Drago Nikolic personally. They asked whether anyone else could receive me. I replied that I had to convey this information to Drago Nikolic in person whereupon they called over another superior officer. I don't know exactly who he was. I did not know officers from that particular department. I suppose it was a security and intelligence department officer who assigned two policemen for my escort. They told me that Drago Nikolic was not at the headquarters at that time and that he was at the forward command post. The police officers, they said, would escort me to the forward command post where Drago Nikolic was. We got back into my car. We went to the forward command post, and finally found Drago Nikolic there. When I reached him at the forward command post, I conveyed Beara's orders to him. I told him that I had been sent by Colonel Beara to convey his order concerning the prisoners, that they should be in Zvornik by that evening, that they would be transferred there, that it was up to him to secure the accommodation and people to guard those prisoners. When we finished talking, I also told him that I had information that the people being transferred to Zvornik would be killed in Zvornik following their detention. Those, I said, were Colonel Beara's orders. I spent about ten minutes talking to Drago Nikolic. Drago Nikolic then told me that he couldn't be on his way right off but that he would consult with his superiors, that he would ask for replacement at the forward command post from the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. The conversation lasted for about ten minutes. I drove back to the Zvornik Brigade. I left the police officer behind at the gate, at the reception. And after that, I drove back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time did you first arrive at the Zvornik Brigade on your way up to see Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, I arrived at half past 9.00 in the evening, or rather, quarter to 10.00 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you escorted by one police officer or two from the Zvornik Brigade headquarters to the Zvornik Brigade forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this a civilian policeman or a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military policeman wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Earlier in the transcript, he indicated that he was provided with two for the escort. Then for some reason, perhaps Mr. McCloskey didn't hear the answer or forgot about it, he was asked another question. But the way the question was phrased, was it one or was it two, that's leading in nature. Perhaps Mr. McCloskey didn't like the previous one. Perhaps he wishes to have the gentleman correct his answer. And I would appreciate it if he would not ask leading questions so we could have a nice clean transcript from which I can cross-examine the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is that an important factor here, one policeman or two policemen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. Maybe Mr. McCloskey could clarify it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my view, there was some confusion whether or not he meant one or two, and at what point. I know what he has said in his statement of facts and other things, so I thought I would ask the question the way I asked it to clarify it. And that's just a normal part of direct examination, to try to clarify the issues so the Court when they're reviewing it and his other statements they can evaluate it. That's purely what I was doing. I've done that before, and I will attempt to continue to keep things as clear as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No doubt he's trying to clarify the record, Your Honour, but there's a way of doing it. You said that, you know, you were provided with two policeman to escort you. How many police officers did in fact escort you, nice and plain. Not, was it one, was it two? This is a multiple choice, and I think it's suggestive. And it may not seem important here, but later on I don't want to give the impression that this is tolerated behaviour that you can ask these sort of leading questions, and I'm trying to be as professional as possible in trying to have a nice, clear, direct examination from Mr. McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas, but I don't think this matter is extremely important. But your intervention may be a warning to the Prosecutor for the future questions. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record, I'm told that the B/C/S language, there was never a mention of two police officers. So this is something that we got in English, which happens. And that's why sometimes I have to clear things up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way back to Bratunac that evening, what route did you take?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the way back to Bratunac, I took the same route, Bratunac, Drinjaca, Konjevic Polje, Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on that route see any other vehicles coming in the other direction?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw several buses coming from Konjevic Polje in the direction of Zvornik. I saw those buses in the region of the village of Kuslata.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see who was in those buses?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could see. And what I saw was that these were captured Muslims who were being transported along that route, going from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time did you get back to Bratunac that night?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, I returned to Bratunac around midnight, maybe a little earlier. But around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you got back to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got back to Bratunac, I went to the Fontana Hotel, and I reported to Colonel Beara telling him that I had relayed his order in its entirety to Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody around when you reported this information to Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I found Colonel Beara in the hotel. He was alone, and the two of us were alone when I reported to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation -- the security situation around town that night in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, when I returned to Bratunac the situation was extremely tense in the security sense. And I can also say that when I returned, there were buses that kept coming, buses and trucks from Nova Kasaba, Milici, towards Bratunac. I can also tell you that everyone was on his feet when I returned and that in Bratunac, it was rather chaotic. That is, the overall situation in Bratunac was rather chaotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it chaotic? Can you explain the problem or the situation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. There were -- in Bratunac, in the facilities I have already listed, the school, the hangar, the secondary school centre, the gym, all these facilities contained a large number of Muslims. That evening, a large number of trucks and buses full of Muslim prisoners had arrived in Bratunac from those directions. And the main problem was that there wasn't sufficient manpower, soldiers and police officers, to secure all those imprisoned Muslims who, objectively speaking, were a danger for the town of Bratunac itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate of how many Muslim prisoners do you think were being held in the town of Bratunac that evening.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my own estimate and based on what I heard that evening, there were between three and a half and four and a half thousand men in Bratunac that evening. Those were the assessments at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that, when you were with Drago Nikolic in the Zvornik area, did you provide him with any kind of an estimate of how many Muslims would be coming up to his area? Muslim prisoners, that is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Drago Nikolic at the time that we were talking about a large number of prisoners, several thousand of them. But I really didn't specify whether it was two, three, or five thousand. I said that we were talking about several thousand Muslims who were in Bratunac at the time, and there were more coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Getting back to the Hotel Fontana that night when you reported to Colonel Beara, what happened? What was said after you gave your report of what you had just been doing?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. Colonel Beara was also worried about the situation. He told me that precisely because of that situation, he had a scheduled meeting with Miroslav Deronjic in the premises of his party. And after that, he invited me to join him and go to the premises of the SD party to see Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Colonel Beara and myself, after I had informed him about the assignment I had carried out, we went to Miroslav Deronjic's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you find Mr. Deronjic present at his office?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we found him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was discussed there? First of all - sorry - let me ask you: Who else was present at the office when you arrived at Deronjic's office that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to Colonel Beara and Miroslav Deronjic and myself, Colonel Vasic, the chief of the centre of the security services in Zvornik was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any security people for Beara or any other people around the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. When we attended that meeting, nobody secured us. There may have been someone in a part of the building, but I really didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What was said by whom at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, the dominant atmosphere was concern over the situation in Bratunac. At that same meeting, Miroslav Deronjic tried to impose his view, which was that the Muslims who were in Bratunac at the time and who were still arriving, that they had to be transported out of Bratunac that very same night. And he opposed any idea of executions and killings taking place in and around Bratunac. Then, also there was a discussion as to the measures to be taken to secure and provide security in town during that night and in the morning. Also, what I heard was that Miroslav Deronjic said that he had already spoken to President Karadzic, and that he had his directives and orders to the effect that all those prisoners should be transported towards Zvornik. And one of the questions discussed was that that evening, all the -- the entire police force of the MUP of Republika Srpska should be engaged as well as free -- soldiers who were free, the military police. And in view of the very serious situation, that volunteers should be called in to assist in the security; that is, all the manpower available should be used to secure the Muslims who were in buses, trucks, in front of the schools, in the side roads. Anyway, in the very centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought up the killing of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The killing of the prisoners was mentioned by Colonel Beara. And at that meeting, there was open discussion about those Muslims who had been captured would later be killed. I told you that the problem discussed was whether this should be done in Bratunac, in Zvornik, or somewhere else. And there was a lot of debate and dispute and argument about this between Colonel Beara and Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Previously, you had mentioned a couple of locations, the brick factory and the Sase mine. Did those places ever come up in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that meeting, no specific sites of execution were mentioned. At least, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any resolution or decision made while you were present in the -- at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A final decision was taken, or rather, there were no real conclusions. But at least that was my impression, that all security measures should be taken that evening to secure the Muslims and the town until the next day, that is, until the 14th, when the process of their transfer to the territory of Zvornik Municipality would begin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible to have continued to send people up to Zvornik that night?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, as I already told you, during that night, I learned that a convoy had left along a different route from the one I took to go to Zvornik, and that is Bratunac, the bridge across the Drina, Drinjaca, but downstream along the Drina. However, that night, it was not possible to continue with the transportation because we didn't have enough manpower which was needed to escort the buses and trucks on their way to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That night, the night of the 13th, early morning hours of the 14th, what forces were guarding the Muslim prisoners at what locations, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I know the following: That the Vuk Karadzic primary school was secured by the military police, that is, members of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. And the school was already full at the time, and I know that Commander Jankovic, Mirko Jankovic, conveyed to me that elements of the MUP from the public security station had been added to the security. I also know that the other facilities where Muslims were being held, the secondary school building, for instance, the hangar building, the gym which was part of the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, that those premises and those Muslim prisoners were being secured by the police force. I also know that the trucks and buses that were arriving along that road were being secured by both members of the civilian police force and that that evening, a large number of volunteers were organised who were called in to take part in securing those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've mentioned police forces and civilian police forces. Can you, as you know, the Ministry of the Interior had different sorts of police forces that you have described for us earlier. To your knowledge, can you explain to us a little more which -- distinguish the various forces of the Ministry of the Interior police.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already explained that. But let me tell you again. As far as I know, within the MUP forces was a special MUP brigade. This is one kind of police force. Then there were units of the so-called PJP police units. And there were also MUP members who were part of the municipal public security stations. The special MUP brigade is a combat unit of the MUP which is formed as follows: Young, able-bodied men, they have personal weapons, mostly automatic weapons. There are also artillery pieces within that unit, and also armoured vehicles or heavy artillery, if I can call them that, tanks, APCs, Pragas, and the rest. Then there are the PJP units --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nikolic, sorry. My question, what I meant to ask you was do you know which of those units were involved in guarding prisoners in Bratunac the evening of 13 July and 14 July? Were there special police brigade units in Bratunac guarding prisoners? Were there PJP units? Was it the civilian police? Could you tell us? You've mentioned police. We just want to know, if you do know, which units of the police were in Bratunac that evening guarding prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which units of the police only? Of the Ministry of the Interior, is that what you mean, Mr. McCloskey? I don't quite understand the question. Are you asking me about units of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any special police units, the people you have described under the command of Dusko Jevic and Mr. Borovcanin? Were any of those units guarding prisoners in Bratunac this evening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really am unable to confirm which exact units were guarding the prisoners because that evening I wasn't there and I don't know. But I can tell you on the basis of what Miodrag Josipovic told me, and what we discussed after the 14th, I can just tell you what I'm saying, that whatever was available from municipal units, PJP units, elements that they took out of their regular duties to guard the prisoners were providing security in that area. I can't tell you exactly which unit belonging to which force was deployed where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of those police units wear blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt, but the gentleman indicated that he wasn't there or he didn't check to see which units. Now he's being asked about a uniform. Now, if this is sort of just a broad question on what kind of uniforms the police wore and the types of uniforms, that's fine. But if the question is directed as to which type of uniform the police officers guarding the prisoners on that particular night, what this gentleman didn't see, if that's the question, then I definitely object to it because it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Mr. Karnavas. Maybe, Mr. McCloskey, it's time for a break. Maybe we could break here, then you think over your question during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, what colour uniforms do municipal police officers normally wear?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal police uniforms, normally wear blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your meeting at the SDS office with Beara and Mr. Deronjic, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that meeting, I went to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. I went straight to the operations room there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the operations room, I found virtually all the officers from the brigade command, or most of them. I told the officers what had to be done. Actually, I told them that we had to bear out the night until the next morning, and I told them that all the prisoners in Bratunac were expected to be transported the next day to the territory of Zvornik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with your commander that evening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That evening, Commander Blagojevic was also in the operations room. And I can also say that I told him separately about what was going on in town, the things I knew. I also told him that I had been in Zvornik. I told him what I had been doing in Zvornik. I conveyed to him the same that I had told the commanding officers, that we had to bear out until the next day. And I told him that the meeting I had attended, a decision had been taken for all the potential -- that all the men available should be engaged to guard the people coming to the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you meet individually with your commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the operations room. I told him all that in the operations room. And particularly, what I had just -- what I just told you. This was after 12.00, maybe 12.30, 12.45. Roughly about that time. Actually, to make myself clearer, it was 45 minutes after midnight. So that would already be the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a separate meeting with Commander Blagojevic that evening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A separate meeting? As far as I can remember, I did not have. I'm not sure about it. It was separate in the sense that I told Commander Blagojevic himself and the members of the brigade command who were present in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your previous answer, you said -- when I asked you, did you meet with your commander that evening, you said: "Yes, that evening Commander Blagojevic was also in the operations room, and I can also say that I told him separately about what was going on in town." And then you go on. When you say "separately," can you clarify what you mean by "separately"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I meant I wasn't talking to all of them in the operations room. The two of us stood aside in the operations room, and then I told him what had been going on. Actually, I conveyed to him everything I had done that evening and what we were to expect as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to need you to tell us as best you can recall particularly what you told him that night.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that upon orders from Colonel Beara, I had gone to Zvornik. I told him the substance of the order which I conveyed to Drago Nikolic in Zvornik. I then told him that I had attended a meeting in the SDS office in Bratunac. After that, I told him what was discussed at that meeting. I also told him that we had to prevail until the next day, the 14th, when the transportation to Zvornik would begin. I told him also what I knew as to what would happen when the people were transported to Zvornik within the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain what do you mean, you knew what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Muslims who were held prisoner in Bratunac would be transported on the 14th to Zvornik and that in Zvornik, they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that that information or that order I had received from Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell him about the killings that were discussed between you and Deronjic and Vasic and Beara at the SDS office?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did tell him about the meeting and about what was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his response when you told him that all these Muslims were going to be killed up in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no reaction or comment on his part. There was no reaction or comments on what I had informed him about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do after providing that information to your commander Blagojevic that evening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I went to the military police building. I conferred with the military police commander and looked into the possibilities there were for further engagement of the military police platoon on guarding the buildings and buses where the Muslim prisoners were being held. There were no policemen available to provide security there because they had all been assigned to other tasks that had been designed on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include guarding the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I was talking about. The possibility for more military policemen of the Bratunac Brigade to provide security where the Muslims were being held in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. It was late, and I went to sleep after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you on duty next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My next duty was on the 14th. I first went to the Fontana Hotel to check security there, the police security. After, that I stayed a while, and I went to the secondary school centre, the new school, secondary school centre where members of UNPROFOR had been transferred to and guarded by military police. Having made that round, between 9.00 and half past 9.00, I left for the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do anything then. I can tell you what I found on my way to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was on my way, I saw in front of me a column forming, a columns of trucks, buses. The transport to Zvornik was underway from the schools and other facilities where the Muslim prisoners had been detained. At the head of that column, I saw a white APC. I parked my car near the bus stop, near a widening of the road in Bratunac. I watched the convoy form and depart for Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what this white APC did?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mirko Jankovic, when he returned from Zvornik, informed me that the white APC was at the head of the column escorting the Muslim prisoners being transferred to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mirko Jankovic tell you what his involvement was in any of this, this transporting to -- the Muslims to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He told me that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic had ordered him to take the APC and to provide security at the front of the column. His task was to see the convoy safely to designated places in Zvornik where the Muslim prisoners would again be detained. And after having seen them there safely, he would return. That was his task. That was his involvement in seeing the column of prisoners get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you any other information about what he had done there, what had happened along the way, or in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He informed me that he had reached certain features, or rather, villages in Zvornik Municipality. He saw the prisoners coming off the buses and walking to those buildings where they were being accommodated, schools and other buildings. He didn't give me the exact location of those villages. He probably didn't know. Then he said that policemen from the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade were taking part in the transport and securing the transport as well as the buses in which the prisoners were being transferred to Zvornik. That was what he told me upon his return from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day did he give you this information and what time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information concerning the escort of the convoy and his own involvement, he gave me this information on the same day when he returned to Zvornik on the 14th in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information about any Bratunac MPs staying in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received information on the 17th, late in the day, the 17th, that a military police patrol escorting the Muslim prisoners had stayed behind in Bilica to provide security for the Muslims who were detained in one of the buildings there in Bilica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say military police patrol, how many military police officers would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally a patrol would comprise two or three men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what days they stayed over in this area, up in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed on the 17th. As for what Mirko told me, I think they stayed for about two days. I think they stayed for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which two days?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the 14th and the 15th, or the 15th and the 16th, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about bodies of Muslims around the school areas in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what information you received.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information that during the night, between the 13th and the 14th, there had been killings of Muslims, that some people had been taken off the buses and that Muslims who had been staying in the hangar had been killed. I received information that between 80 and a hundred Muslims had been killed that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this information from the commander of the civilian affairs unit, Dragan Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what the commander of the civilian affairs unit, what his normal responsibilities are just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibilities of the commander of the civilian affairs unit for the most part entailed tasks of clearing the terrain, clearing the area in which combat activities and other activities took place, clearing buildings and territory in which captured or detained Muslims were being held. Cleaning and burial of bodies found as a result of combat operations or otherwise killed. That would amount to his tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the B/C/S term "asanacija". Can you define what that term means in particular.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The B/C/S term asanacija is one of the measures from the general area of civilian protection. It entails the clearing of terrain, removing dead bodies, removing animals that had been killed or burned. In one word, it involves clearing both the terrain and the buildings and removing everything that could cause epidemics or diseases later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the commander of the civilian affairs unit, Dragan Mirkovic, identify who he believed killed these Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dragan Mirkovic did not tell me who had killed the Muslims. He told me what he knew about the dead bodies that had been found on the 14th, or rather, the Muslims that had been killed between the 13th and the 14th. He told me that the civilian bodies, the civilian government requested for him to provide a vehicle so that the dead bodies of the Muslims that had been killed could be put away during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to your commander Blagojevic on the 14th as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak to Commander Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you speak to him about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I must say on the 14th, no official meeting with Colonel Blagojevic took place. However, we talked mainly about what I had found out in relation to those killed at the Vuk Karadzic elementary school and the situation that night. Of course, we also talked about the transport and about the involvement of our members from the military police, Mirko Jankovic, in the transport of the captured persons in the Zvornik territory, Zvornik municipal territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagojevic have any further instructions or comments to you relating to what you had told him about, the things you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I know. And I think my recollection is quite clear. There were no specific instructions or orders or directives regarding what I had informed him about. And he was aware of these things himself, even without me informing him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know that? I'm not sure I understand the question. How do I know that he had been informed, or how do I know that he issued me instructions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that he was informed of this information that you had been providing him? Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I know this because the transport operation, the operation of detaining persons and everything that was going on in town in those days, was so comprehensive, was so large scale, the logistic support and everything else that was happening, most of the Bratunac Brigade officers took part in that. Organs of the Bratunac Brigade took part, and some of the units of the Bratunac Brigade took part. It is normal that a commander in that situation would know what was going on in town. Furthermore, this was all happening in the centre of town, in the town of Bratunac. It would have been normal for a brigade commander to know what was happening in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Beara left the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when your commander Blagojevic left the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and to the best of my recollection, roughly speaking, it was on the 17th of July, 1995. That's when Commander Blagojevic left for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he take some troops with him to take part in the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know roughly when he returned?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, and this is all I can give you, I think he returned after the fall of Zepa. I'm not sure whether it was -- I don't know the exact date, but I know it was after the fall of Zepa that he returned. But I know nothing about Zepa itself, so I can't give you the exact date of his return. I know it was certainly after the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if it was in July or August or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we go back to the multiple choice, you know, trying to help the witness out. It's leading. If the gentleman said he doesn't remember. Now, if he has got something to refresh his memory, I would welcome that opportunity. There's no problem with that. But this giving the witness multiple choice suggestive answers, I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we have to know roughly during which months that your client came back. I understand the witness said he did not know the exact date. But it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you more, Your Honour, but there may be a way other than giving suggestive answers, perhaps, to refresh the gentleman's memory because after all, the Prosecutor has been working on this case for eight years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think this issue is of crucial importance for your client. And in these circumstances, the questions with certain leading elements are allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I gave you several options of months. Any idea what month he may have been back in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he returned at some point in July, after the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, did you receive information that bodies in the Bratunac Brigade zone should be dug up and moved to some other locations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received that information, or rather instructions in September, at some point in September. I can't tell you the exact date, September 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you received those instructions from.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received those instructions from the chief of security of the Drina Corps, Mr. Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Popovic tell you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Popovic told me then that the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska had ordered him to transfer the bodies of the Muslims who had been buried in the village of Glogovi to a set of new locations in Srebrenica Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened after he told you that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he told me that, another thing I wish to tell you is that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic also told me on that occasion that I would be in charge of coordinating activities in that respect and that fuel for this operation would be provided by the main staff and command of the Drina Corps. Further, he told me that the 5th engineering battalion of the Drina Corps would take part in the operation with their equipment. He said that the civilian police would also take part in the operation. He told me that security for the operation, that's between the graves in Glogovi and the transfer of these dead bodies to Srebrenica Municipality, would be provided by members of the military police from the Bratunac Brigade. He said as the logistical support of the 5th engineering battalion would not be sufficient, we should get in touch with the civilian authorities to try to secure additional heavy equipment and trucks that would be necessary for the operation. After I had received this task and after I had been told what I had been told by Mr. Popovic, I informed Colonel Blagojevic accordingly telling him also that we should get in touch with the civilian authorities. I obtained authorisation from Colonel Blagojevic to contact the president of Bratunac Municipality, the president of the Executive Board, and the chief of the MUP, the Bratunac MUP. I did so, and a meeting was organised at the Municipal Assembly building in Bratunac with the chief of the MUP ministry in Bratunac, Mr. Vespovic in attendance, as well as president of the municipality Ljubisa Simic, president of the executive board of Bratunac, Srbislav Davidovic, and myself. They assumed the responsibility to talk to presidents of those companies which actually owned the heavy equipment. That heavy equipment would be commandeered, they said, and used in the operation. Heavy equipment from the following companies was used: Socially owned enterprise, Bratunac Brickworks; communal state company Komunalno Bratunac; heavy equipment and trucks from both companies were used. Trucks were used belonging to the state-owned company Sase mine; from Autoprevoz Srebrenica, trucks were taken from them. A digger was taken from a state-owned construction company, Radnik, based in Srebrenica. After this, the graves were dug up in the village of Glogova, and the bodies were moved to new gravesites in Srebrenica Municipality. As for the officers of the Bratunac Brigade who took part in that operation, I, for one, coordinated the functioning of the entire operation. Assistant chief of intelligence Jovanovic, Dragisa, also took part. Commander of the military police platoon Mirko Jankovic also took part, as well as the whole military police platoon depending on the specific day of the operation because the operation did go on for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
